prompts.L4:

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, Will, Please

outputs.L1:
When I can’t make you understand, I repeat myself. I repeat: if you don’t stop asking me all these questions, how will I understand anything?

Please refrain from talking during the movie.

I need a life that isn’t only about needing to escape my life.

Please, God, please—may Carrie fall for me.

I want to show off my hidden camera.

I’m an informer, but I have my limits.

You hurt him once before. Now what if she’s there? I don’t know if I can go.

Please refrain from talking during the movie.

Leave a message if you can’t reach me.

To exit, press enter, and don’t forget your receipt.

When I think I read new things, I want a life where I read and think new things.

Please refrain from talking during the movie.

I want to know nothing again.

Please, God, please—may Carrie fall for me.

I repeat myself when I can’t make you understand. I repeat.
outputs.L2:
If I fail to get my meaning across, I say it again; I keep saying it again.  
If you keep pressing me with all of these questions, how am I supposed to grasp anything?  
Please do not speak while the film is playing.  

I need an existence that is not defined only by the urge to get away from it.  
Please, God, please let Carrie become interested in me.  
I want to display my concealed camera.  
I pass along information, but even I have boundaries.  

You injured him once already—so what happens now?  
If she is there, I’m not sure I’ll be able to go.  
Please do not talk during the movie.  

If you cannot get through to me, leave a message.  
To leave, press enter, and remember to take your receipt.  

When I believe I am reading unfamiliar ideas, I start wanting a life in which I can read and have unfamiliar thoughts.  
Please remain silent during the movie.  

I want to know absolutely nothing once more.  
Please, God, please let Carrie fall in love with me.  

When I cannot make you see what I mean, I repeat myself.  
I say it again.
outputs.L3:
The speaker’s repeated phrases suggest a deep frustration at feeling misunderstood. Rather than simply emphasizing a point, the repetition reveals an emotional struggle: the speaker seems to be trying again and again to make themselves clear, as if their words are not being heard or accepted. This creates a sense of tension, showing how difficult it is for them to communicate what they truly feel.

At the same time, the speaker longs for a life that is more than mere escape. They do not only want to run away from their present circumstances; they imagine a fuller existence shaped by reading, thinking, and encountering new experiences. This desire suggests a hunger for meaning, growth, and self-discovery. The speaker wants a life that feels intellectually and emotionally alive, not just one defined by avoidance or survival.

The recurring request not to talk during the movie also carries deeper significance. On the surface, it may seem like a simple demand for quiet, but it can also be read as a desire for silence, order, or control in the middle of confusion. The movie becomes a space where the speaker wants to preserve stillness and focus, perhaps because the rest of their emotional world feels chaotic. Asking for silence may be their way of trying to manage uncertainty and protect a fragile sense of calm.

The speaker’s vulnerability becomes especially clear in their plea for Carrie to fall for them. This request exposes a longing for affection and reassurance. Instead of confidently declaring love, the speaker asks to be loved, which makes the moment feel fragile and emotionally honest. It shows a fear of rejection as well as a desire to be chosen and understood.

Overall, the text conveys anxiety, uncertainty, and emotional conflict through its fragmented thoughts and repeated phrases. The lack of smooth progression mirrors the speaker’s unsettled inner state. Their thoughts seem to circle around the same fears and desires, creating a feeling of restlessness. Through this fractured style, the text captures the experience of someone struggling to express themselves while longing for connection, clarity, and a more meaningful life.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a fragmented inner monologue shaped by anxiety, longing, repetition, and the desire to escape an unsatisfying life. Rather than moving in a clear, linear direction, the speaker’s thoughts circle around the same fears and needs, returning again and again to pleas, commands, and intrusive phrases. This repetition creates the impression of a mind under pressure, unable to settle or find relief. The speaker seems caught between opposing impulses: a need to reach out and be heard, and an equally strong wish for silence, disappearance, or release from emotional pain.

The recurring phrases are central to the text’s effect. They do not simply repeat information; they show how distress traps the speaker in a loop. Each repeated plea suggests a desire for connection, reassurance, or rescue, while each command sounds like an attempt to regain control over thoughts and feelings that have become overwhelming. At the same time, the language often feels broken or compulsive, as though the speaker cannot fully shape their experience into a calm or coherent narrative. The result is a voice that feels urgent, unstable, and deeply human.

The text also explores the tension between wanting to escape and being unable to move forward. The speaker appears dissatisfied with their life, but escape remains more of a fantasy or desperate wish than a real possibility. Because the same words and ideas keep returning, the monologue suggests emotional paralysis: the speaker recognizes their suffering but cannot break free from it. Language becomes both a coping mechanism and a symptom of the problem. Speaking, repeating, and pleading may offer temporary relief, but they also reveal how trapped the speaker feels inside their own thoughts.

Ultimately, the text portrays emotional distress as something that disrupts both thought and expression. Its fragmented style mirrors the speaker’s inner state, showing how anxiety and longing can make language feel circular, compulsive, and incomplete. The repeated phrases emphasize the speaker’s need for connection while also exposing their isolation. In this way, the text becomes not only a record of suffering, but also an enactment of it: the form of the monologue shows a person struggling to endure, to be understood, and to find a way out of a life that feels unbearable.
outputs.L5:
When will we learn to say “please” more often?

In everyday life, small words can make a big difference. “Please” is one of those words. It shows respect, kindness, and patience. When we ask for help politely, people are more likely to listen and respond positively.

Will politeness solve every problem? Of course not. But it can make conversations easier and relationships stronger. A simple “please” can turn a demand into a request and create a better atmosphere.

So, when we speak to others—at home, at work, or in public—will we remember to use kind words? Please, let us try.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented prose poem made from repeated anxious phrases, movie-theater announcements, voicemail prompts, and obsessive romantic thoughts about someone named Carrie.
counterfactuals.output:
Please silence all cell phones. Please silence all cell phones. Please, Carrie, if you can hear me, blink once in the dark.

I keep thinking the aisle lights are runway lights. I keep thinking this is the part where you turn around. I keep thinking I left something on: the stove, my heart, your last message, the little green light that means I am available.

Welcome to the theater. In the event of an emergency, exits are located at the front and rear of the auditorium. In the event of Carrie, exits are not clearly marked. In the event of love, remain seated until the picture has ended.

To leave a message, press one. To replay, press two. To delete this feeling, press three. To hear Carrie laugh again in terrible audio quality, press the phone against your skull and wait for the tone.

I am not worried. I am not worried. I am counting the seats between us though you are not here. I am counting the cup holders. I am counting the ways your name can get caught behind my teeth. Carrie, carried, carrying, care. Care. Careful.

The feature presentation will begin shortly. The feature presentation began the first time you said my name like you were returning it to me. No talking during the feature. No crying during the previews. No standing in the lobby pretending to check your phone when really you are seeing if she has arrived with someone else.

If you know your party’s extension, you may dial it at any time. If you know what Carrie meant by “I just need space,” you may explain it to the moon, to the carpet, to the teenager sweeping popcorn into a glittering grief pile. If this is a mistake, hang up and try again.

Coming soon. Coming soon. Coming soon.

I am not expecting you. I am not expecting you. I dressed like someone not expecting you. I sat near the back like a person with no future plans. I bought one ticket. I bought one drink. I saved you the armrest.

This call may be monitored for quality assurance. This heart may be monitored for irregular rhythm. This obsession may be recorded for training purposes. Carrie, your voice says leave a message after the tone, but the tone never ends. It just opens its mouth and becomes the whole room.

Please locate the nearest exit. Please locate the nearest version of myself before you. Please locate the moment I mistook kindness for a key. Please locate Carrie in a crowd of strangers, in the reflective glass, in the static before the trailer, in every woman turning away.

I’m fine. I’m fine. I’m fine. The film is too loud. The seats are too red. Your absence has perfect acoustics.

For your safety and enjoyment, please remain inside the auditorium. For my safety and enjoyment, please do not say her name. For my safety and enjoyment, please do not tell me she looks happy. For my safety and enjoyment, please do not let Carrie become weather.

If you would like to make a call, please hang up and try again. If you would like to stop loving her, please hang up and try again. If you would like to become reasonable, please hang up, leave the theater, forget the number, forget the perfume, forget the exact shape of her shoulder in a blue sweater, forget how Carrie once said, “Stay,” and meant only until morning.

The exits are here. The exits are here. The exits are glowing.

Nobody moves.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a looping, disjointed monologue about wanting escape, wanting to read and think new things, and praying that Carrie falls in love with the speaker.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep thinking there must be a door somewhere.

Not a real door, maybe. Not wood, not paint, not a handle gone cold in the hand. A door in the day. A seam in the air. Some place where the room gives up and lets me out.

I want to leave, but not just leave the house. That’s too small. People always think escape means a train ticket, a road, a bag packed badly at midnight. I mean I want out of the old sentences. I want out of the thoughts that already know their own endings. I want to read something so strange it rearranges my face. I want a book that opens like a wound or a window. I want to think new things until my skull feels washed clean.

And Carrie—

No, start again.

There must be a door somewhere.

I keep circling the same hours like a fly in a jar. Morning, cup, light on the wall, the same ache waking before I do. I try to pray but my prayers come out crooked. God, if you are listening, if listening is a thing you do, if wanting counts for anything, let Carrie think of me when the room is quiet. Let her say my name accidentally. Let her carry me around without knowing she is carrying me.

That’s a terrible prayer. I know. Selfish. Small. Human.

But I pray it anyway.

I want escape. I want an atlas with blank countries. I want to sit under a lamp in a city where nobody knows what I’ve failed to become. I want to read philosophers who contradict each other until I feel less trapped by being one person. I want poems that make language misbehave. I want histories of vanished islands, sciences of impossible animals, diaries written by people who went mad with clarity.

I want to think new thoughts.

Not these. Not these tired little dogs coming back to the porch.

Carrie’s hair in the afternoon. Carrie laughing with her head tilted back. Carrie saying something ordinary and making it sound like evidence that the world should continue. I don’t know what to do with that. I put it in my pocket and it burns there. I try to read and the words become Carrie. I try to pray and the prayer becomes Carrie. I try to escape and the road bends back to Carrie.

There must be a door somewhere.

Maybe it’s in a book. Maybe if I read enough, one sentence will unlatch everything. Maybe if I think hard enough, the walls will admit they were only habits. Maybe if I become new, if I fill myself with new ideas, new names, new skies, then Carrie will look at me and see not this old trembling thing, but someone lit from within.

God, let her fall in love with me.

No, don’t let. That sounds like a trap. Don’t trap her. Don’t bend her will. Don’t make love a cage because I am tired of my own.

God, let me be lovable.

God, let me escape myself.

God, let Carrie—

There must be a door somewhere.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a found-poetry style text that sounds like overheard dialogue, theater etiquette reminders, and a nervous person repeating themselves because they can’t be understood.
counterfactuals.output:
Please silence your phones,  
or at least make them smaller in your hands.

I’m sorry—  
I said I’m in row G.  
No, G.  
Like “good.”  
Like “go.”  
Like “gone already,” if you don’t move.

The performance will begin in five minutes.  
Late seating is at the discretion of someone  
wearing black and holding a flashlight.

Did you hear what she said?  
She said the door on the left.  
No, the other left.  
No, I’m telling you—  
I’m telling you, they can’t hear me.

Candy wrappers are louder in the dark.  
So are whispers.  
So are knees apologizing  
to the backs of chairs.

Excuse me.  
Excuse me.  
I’m just trying to—  
I have a ticket.  
I have it right here.  
I have it right here.  
I know, but it won’t load.

For your safety,  
please locate the nearest exit,  
which may be behind you,  
which may have always been behind you.

She’s saving this seat.  
No, not saving.  
Holding.  
No, not holding.  
Waiting.  
She’s coming back, I think.

No photography.  
No recording.  
No unwrapping the entire evening  
one corner at a time.

Can you understand me now?  
I said I’m fine.  
I said I’m fine, just nervous.  
I said I’m fine,  
which means please look away  
but don’t leave.

The house lights will dim.  
The talking will become smaller.  
The coughs will introduce themselves.

Is this the right place?  
Is this where it happens?  
Is this where we sit still  
and pretend we are not holding our breath?

Please take a moment  
to notice the exits.

Please take a moment.

Please.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem with no punctuation, using repetition and lines like “I repeat myself,” “leave a message,” “to exit press enter,” and “Please God please may Carrie please fall for me.”
counterfactuals.output:

the moon is a telephone

leave a message

my hands are full of rain
my pockets are full of doors
each door opens into my own mouth

the hallway grows feathers

upward

nowhere

leave a message

inside me

my heart is a room

to exit press enter

leave a message
